HEADLINE: CFMEU must 'clean own house first'
TEXT:
Senior Construction, Forestry, Maritime, Mining and Energy Union officials, including those who backed John Setka despite his harassment conviction, previously advocated that the union cannot accept abuse against women.

Just weeks after sending dozens of abusive text messages to his wife last year, Mr Setka appeared with CFMEU national secretary Michael O'Connor and other senior leaders from his union in a campaign video to denounce domestic violence.

The video, published on November 25, kick-started the CFMEU's 16 days of activism over the issue but now exposes the stark contradictions facing the union after its Victorian secretary pleaded guilty this week to harassing his wife.

Outspoken Setka supporters, CFMEU NSW president Rita Mallia, CFMEU WA secretary Mick Buchan and MUA national president Christy Cain all speak in the video saying "no to violence against women".

ALP vice-president and head of the maritime division women's committee, Michelle Myers, also appears following an image saying "one in four Australian women has experienced emotional abuse by a current or former partner".

"The CFMEU cannot accept this," she says.

The CFMEU's construction division has given its "full support" to Mr Setka despite calls by the Australian Council of Trade Unions to resign over the harassment charges.

However, the union has also refused to comment on Mr Setka's harassment case, including since his conviction on Wednesday.

Both Ms Myers and Mr O'Connor, who is on the ALP executive, have declined requests to comment on the Setka matter.

Family violence campaigner and columnist Jenna Price said Mr Setka's actions and the CFMEU's refusal to call for his resignation had made a mockery of their family violence campaign.

She said it was apparently not acceptable "unless he's the construction secretary - and then it's fine," she said.

"I'm imagining if they do this [campaign] again it will be along the lines of people making little memes - a yes campaign against domestic violence unless it's in house."

She said she was "astonished" Mr Setka was still in his position and "it is completely staggering to me that [the CFMEU] do not realise the impact this has had on their reputation".

Mr Setka himself appears in the video demanding that the government "go into action to stop violence against women".

But on the last day of the CFMEU's 16-day campaign, he was hit with a family intervention court order that he later breached on three separate occasions. A month before the video, Mr Setka sent his wife Emma Walters 45 text messages in one night, including photos of her face erased with permanent marker and her belongings thrown out.

His texts included calling her a "treacherous Aussie f---n' c---t", "a weak f---n piece of shit" and "a drunken moron". One message said "you just triggered a hatred ... I didn't think existed f---n dog".

Despite facing an intervention order, he would continue sending her messages and call her a "f---n dog" for involving the police.

Domestic Violence Resource Centre chief executive Emily Maguire said now that Mr Setka had pleaded guilty it was up to the CFMEU to "think about what that means for them".

"We often have discussions with organisations who want to campaign on ending family violence, which is fantastic but you've also got to get in there to clean your own house first," she said.

"You can't be spruiking a message without paying attention to your own organisation."

Mr Setka was released on a 12-month good behaviour bond and ordered to undergo a men's behavioural change program and pay $1000 to an Aboriginal domestic violence service.

He apologised to his wife in a statement on Wednesday and said "it's not OK for us to speak to each other like that".

Ms Walters, who complained to police about her husband but did not provide them a victim impact statement, has also come out in support of Mr Setka despite the abuse.

The CFMEU national branch has been associated with the White Ribbon movement and all the maritime division officials are understood to be White Ribbon Ambassadors.

Mr Setka's deputy Shaun Reardon was also a White Ribbon Ambassador before he quit the union last week due to "personal values I will live and die by".

HEADLINE: More businesses will pay for music under new system
TEXT:
The two collection agencies for Australia's music industry are set to raise more revenue from businesses that play their tunes, under a new regime that requires business owners to buy only one music licence instead of the two previously needed.

The profits-to-members agencies, which together collected about $100 million from businesses in 2017-18, claim the income boost will come from proprietors who were confused by the former two-licence regime, and therefore had held only one licence or none.

The agencies claim businesses compliant with the previous regime won't pay any more when the new system, OneMusic, comes into effect on July 1.

Any business that uses music, from nightclubs and restaurants to call centres with hold music, has hitherto had to acquire two licences for it.

One was from the merged Australasian Performing Right Association-Australasian Mechanical Copyright Owners Society (APRA AMCOS), which collects on behalf of member songwriters, music publishers and composers. The other was from the Phonographic Performance Company of Australia (PPCA), which collects on behalf of recording artists and record labels.

From July 1, those licences will merge into a single OneMusic licence, with fees then flowing to each member organisation, generally on a 50-50 basis.

"We know many businesses found it hard to deal with two separate rights organisations and some neglected their obligations altogether," APRA AMCOS chief executive Dean Ormston said.

"A simple, single, easy-to-use system will significantly reduce the administration burden for everyone."

In order not to be seen as "some sort of government impost" by new licensees, Mr Ormston said the OneMusic interface emphasised that music was a product that businesses benefited from paying for.

"The new website will be publishing content about how music can help businesses, and we'll offer advice to any licensee that reaches out to us," he said. "We are selling a product that's proven to make your customers happier and to spend more, and the livelihoods of the people that make that product needs to be protected."

The arrival of OneMusic coincides with calls for APRA AMCOS and PPCA to be more accountable about how fees they collect are distributed.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission recently made the reauthorisation of APRA AMCOS, which with PPCA holds a monopoly over music rights management, contingent on it publishing an annual transparency report with information on rights revenue, operating costs and payments to members.

The Council of Small Business Australia is even pushing for a Senate inquiry into the performance right royalties system.

Mr Ormston promised OneMusic would address transparency and expense concerns, with a new quoting system that allowed business owners to specify how and for how long they used music.

There are 24 types of OneMusic licence, from childcare to workplace music via funeral directors and karaoke. This represents a streamlining from previous arrangements, where APRA AMCOS alone offered 32 licence types.

HEADLINE: Shake-up to boost older workers
TEXT:
Older workers will be encouraged to stay longer in the work force and boost their super savings with a range of new rules that begin on Monday.

They include another increase in the pension and super preservation age that are contributing to higher participation in the workplace by older Australians.

Australians born between January 1, 1954 and June 30, 1955 will have to wait until they turn 66 before they can receive the age pension. This is part of an ongoing schedule to increase the age pension to 67 by July 1, 2023.

In addition, the age superannuation assets can be accessed, known as the preservation age, is also being raised. Individuals turning 57 between July 1, 2019 and June 30, 2020 will have to wait until age 58 (from July 1, 2020) to access their super.

"This will also delay the start of accessing the popular 'Transition to Retirement Pension', where you can access up to 10 per cent of your super as an income stream, to combine with paid work," said John Perri, AMP technical strategy manager.

According to Ernst & Young, women and older Australians are the two groups for which the rise in participation is "particularly pronounced".

"The eligibility age for the pension was progressively raised from 60 to 65 and is now being gradually increased to 67," a spokesman for the consultancy said. "The preservation age at which individuals can access their superannuation is also being gradually increased. These changes are contributing to higher participation by older Australians."

The maximum rate for the age pension, including supplements, is currently $926.20 for a single person per fortnight. If you are a couple, the rate is $698.10 each per fortnight. The "work bonus", which aims to encourage people who've reached pension age to continue doing some paid work, is also getting a boost from $250 per fortnight to $300 before their pension is affected.

"That means a single pensioner can earn a maximum of $474 per fortnight [$300 from employment, $174 from other income] before their pension payments are reduced. The self-employed, like sole traders, will now also be able to apply for the 'work bonus' for the first time," said Mr Perri.

Another change will make eligible retirees aged 65 to 74 with a super balance below $300,000 (as at June 30, 2019) to make voluntary super contributions for 12 months from the end of the financial year in which they last met the work test.

The work test determines eligibility to make personal contributions for those aged 65 and over and less than 75.

Currently, those eligible to make voluntary super contributions must work a minimum of 40 hours in any 30-day period in a financial year.

"The reason some people make voluntary super contributions at this stage is often to take advantage of the generous tax conditions within super and potentially increase their retirement balances," said Mr Perri. "But this may not be the right strategy for everyone."

Also for the first time, those whose total super balance is below $500,000 as at June 30, 2019, can play super catch up by contributing more pre-tax income to super.

HEADLINE: Coalition gets close to income tax cut deal
TEXT:
Scott Morrison appears on track to secure a significant victory in the first week of the new Parliament, with key Senate crossbenchers declaring a deal on the government's income tax cuts close to completion.

Coalition Senate leader Mathias Cormann is expected to meet with Centre Alliance senators Rex Patrick and Stirling Griff on Monday, part of final stage negotiations for a deal on the $158 billion three-stage tax cut plan.

Senator Patrick, who is leading negotiations on gas supply into the east coast market as the price for the Centre Alliance's support, said he believed the two sides were "relatively close" and the possibility of a vote on Thursday remained open.

"I think we will have some face to face with the government very early next week," he said. "That will be the best way to resolve any of the final speed humps. Sometimes you just have to sit down together in a room."

Analysis by the Parliamentary Budget Office, commissioned by the Greens and released on Friday, showed more than two thirds of the final stage of the package would benefit workers earning below $180,000, further damaging Labor's election campaign claims that wealthy Australians would receive an outsized share of the benefit.

Australians earning more than $180,000 would receive nearly $30 billion of the final stage, worth a total of $95 billion.

Greens leader Richard Di Natale is lobbying returning Tasmanian senator Jacqui Lambie to oppose the cuts, arguing voters in wealthier parts of the country would benefit more than her constituents.

A spokeswoman for Senator Lambie said she would not discuss her position until Parliament sits next week.

Thursday is the first opportunity for a Senate vote, after a ceremonial opening event and condolence motions for former prime minister Bob Hawke on Wednesday.

The government has listed the tax cut package as the first item of business in the Senate, but a delay could see two more weeks of inaction while MPs return to their electorates until July 22.

Labor's shadow treasurer Jim Chalmers on Friday used the release of the Parliamentary Budget Office analysis to attack the Coalition.

"From 2024-25 onwards, 30 to 36 per cent of the benefit of the total tax package goes to 8 to 11 per cent of Australians who are earning more than $180,000," Mr Chalmers said.

"For more than two months the government has refused to provide these numbers to help Parliament consider whether it is responsible to commit that much five years out to people who are least likely to spend it in the economy. The only proposal on the table which will give everyone a tax cut this term is Labor's proposal."

Mr Chalmers echoed Opposition Leader Anthony Albanese's calls for stages one and two to be passed without delay to help stimulate the economy.

"The government should bring forward to 2019-20 an infrastructure package and the increase in the $90,000 threshold to $120,000," he said. "Stage three should be considered at a later date given it wouldn't come in until 2024-25 and we don't know what the economy or the budget will look like."

Home Affairs Minister Peter Dutton said Labor should respect the government's election mandate pass the cuts.

"If Labor support it in the Senate it is a done deal, people have more money in their pockets," he said.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, who remains opposed to the cuts, did not respond to requests for comment on Friday.

Key pointsCentre Alliance senator Rex Patrick says there could be a vote as early as Thursday.

A delay could see two more weeks of inaction while MPs return to their electorates.

HEADLINE: Morrison digs in for long trade war
TEXT:
Osaka: Australia has intensified efforts to strike a free trade deal with the European Union and finalise a new 16-nation Asia-Pacific trade pact to help cushion the impact of what looms as a dangerously protracted US-China trade war.

After meeting US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the G20 leaders' summit in Osaka' Japan, Mr Morrison said there was no prospect of their dispute being resolved when they meet in Osaka today.

"I think it would be unrealistic to expect a resolution tomorrow," he said.

International Monetary Fund chairwoman Christine Lagarde told assembled G20 leaders that if the war escalated and culminated in further tariffs, as Mr Trump is threatening, forecast global growth for calendar year 2020 will be significantly downgraded from 3.6 per cent to 3.1 per cent.

The warning comes after six months in which central banks have become increasingly concerned and global markets have soared on the resulting cheap money.

Mr Morrison said Australia and the other G20 nations, while doing what they could to end the dispute between the superpowers, were not prepared to "just sit there and wait for some sort of resolution". "We need a clear-eyed understanding of where we are at," he said.

"We just get on with it with the many other relationships that we have."

"Two of the biggest running right now for us and for this year are the Regional Economic Comprehensive Partnership (RCEP), which is principally driven out of ASEAN, as well as our efforts to land an agreement with the EU. Continuing to be active on these other trade agendas while at the same time appreciating the impact of the biggest bilateral relationship having tensions and what that means for the global economy, are the practical things that we do to respond."

While the leaders met in Osaka, trade representatives from 16 RCEP nations were in Melbourne for talks. They were from the 10 ASEAN nations as well as China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand and India.

The goal is to conclude RCEP by the end of the year while there is no timeline on the EU deal other than to finalise it as soon as is practicable.

Mr Morrison said the global situation was worse now than at the previous G20 in Argentina in December. Back then, Mr Trump and Mr Xi met and agreed to a 90-day ceasefire that ultimately ended without resolution.

Mr Trump more than doubled import tariffs on $US200 billion of Chinese goods from 10 per cent to 25 per cent and has threatened to impose tariffs on another $US300 billion of goods.

"It's more important, it's serious and the IMF reminded G20 members of how serious," Mr Morrison said of the situation compared with that in Buenos Aires. "It's the difference between 3.6 per cent and 3.1 per cent on global economic growth."

Other G20 leaders expressed similar concerns. Summit host and Japanese Prime Minster Shinzo Abe said he harboured "grave concerns" about the situation with global trade. He said World Trade Organisation reform was needed to maintain the multilateral trading system which, in turn, was fundamental to peace and prosperity.

Mr Morrison told fellow leaders during the G20 trade talks that one in five Australian jobs depended on trade, the nation was in its 28th year of uninterrupted economic growth, and half the workforce had never known recession. This was off the back of three decades of reforms and Australia was not going to allow that to be jeopardised by a trade war. He repeated his pitch the WTO needed reform to its antiquated rules so it could resolve disputes such as that between China and the US.

During their dinner on Thursday night, Mr Morrison impressed upon Mr Trump the concerns of Australia and other nations of the damage they will suffer as a result of the ongoing dispute.

Sources said Mr Morrison was "forward leaning" in his representation.

He made the same point to Mr Xi.

The US-China dispute is being driven by Chinese practices such as intellectual property theft, industrial subsidies, forced technology transfer and it being able to designate itself developing nation status by the WTO. The US is responding with tariffs.

Mr Xi told leaders of the BRIC group of nations, who he met on the sidelines of the G20, that protectionism was "destroying" the global trade order.

"This also impacts common interests of our countries, overshadows the peace and stability worldwide," Mr Xi said.

European Commission President Jean-Claude Junker said the trade spat threatened global economic growth.

"The trade relations between China and the United States are difficult, they are contributing to the slowdown of the global economy," he said.

China is resolutely resisting change and The Wall Street Journal reported that Mr Xi will present Mr Trump with a list of demands today to which the US is most unlikely to agree.

These included insisting the US remove its ban on the sale of US technology to Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei, lifting all punitive tariffs and dropping efforts to get China to buy even more US exports than Beijing said it would when the two leaders last met in Argentina.

Mr Morrison had a small victory at the G20 when he won the backing of France and Canada for his push to stop social media platforms, such as Facebook, streaming violent terrorist footage, as it did during the Christchurch massacre.

The proposal has met with resistance from some nations who are worried about infringing on freedom of speech. Mr Morrison stressed that was not his intention.

"It's about the internet being weaponised by violent terrorists," he said.

The G20 was also likely, for a second time in succession, to water down the language in the communique concerning climate change to appease the US, which has withdrawn from the Paris agreements.

HEADLINE: Morrison tees up a Trump visit
TEXT:
Scott Morrison has formalised an invitation for Donald Trump to visit Australia in December to coincide with the biennial Presidents Cup golf tournament.

The Australian Financial Review revealed in April the visit, the brainchild of Australia's ambassador to the US, Joe Hockey, was under consideration.

Asked on Thursday night whether he intended to come, Mr Trump was keen but uncommitted.

"I'll tell you what, I'd like to," said Mr Trump, an avid golfer. "It might not be easy, but I'd like to. That's a big deal. That's going to be great."

On Friday, following his Thursday night dinner with Mr Trump and ahead of meeting with other world leaders, Mr Morrison said the invitation to attend the event at Royal Melbourne Golf Club, which has hosted it twice before, would be made formal.

"We did send that invitation and we will issue a formal one," he said.

He was also optimistic Mr Trump would come.

"I think there is a reasonable chance. He is obviously a passionate follower of the sport and the tournament is actually named after the President so I think it would be great for Melbourne and for the tournament," he said.

The Presidents Cup features the best American golfers playing the best golfers from the rest of the world, excluding Europe.

This year, the US team will be captained by Tiger Woods, who was awarded a Presidential Medal of Freedom by Mr Trump in April after winning the US Masters, his 15th major.

If Mr Trump attends the event from December 12-15, he will be the first sitting president to do so outside of the United States.

Royal Melbourne previously hosted the tournament in 1998 and 2011, the only other times it has been held in Australia. In 1998, then-former president George H W Bush attended the event but not the then-president Bill Clinton. The 2011 tournament coincided with a visit to Australia by then-president Barack Obama, also a keen golfer.

But he gave it a wide berth to avoid criticism at home. At the time, his trip abroad also included visits to Hawaii, Bali and the G20 in Cannes. Under domestic pressure over the economy, the spectre of the president at a golf tournament on top of three holiday destinations would not have gone down well, diplomatic sources said.

HEADLINE: We would look at aiding US over Iran: PM
TEXT:
Osaka | Scott Morrison has not ruled out Australia joining the United States in military action against Iran, saying any request would be considered very seriously and on its merits.

The Iran situation was discussed on Thursday night at a dinner between Mr Morrison and Donald Trump that was also attended by administration hawks including US Secretary of State Mike Pompeo and National Security Adviser John Bolton.

Mr Morrison said Australian involvement in any military action "certainly wasn't sought".

"Obviously we talked about these issues and we have been watching them very closely as well, but there are no requests and at this stage I think those issues are a bit premature," he said. "But we are obviously concerned. We would deal with any specific request from an ally such as the United States very seriously and on its merits."

Tensions between the US and Iran are escalating amid allegations from Washington that Tehran has attacked oil tankers in the Straits of Hormuz, was exporting terrorism, shot down a US drone, and has breached its 2015 nuclear deal with the Obama administration from which the Trump administration has walked away.

Last year, Australia under Mr Morrison's new leadership reviewed its support for that deal but made no change.

President Trump, who campaigned for office by attacking the US invasion of Iraq, does not want another war and he declined to retaliate militarily for the shooting down of the drone.

But he is using his stay in Japan for the G20 summit to muster international support for any potential military action. This includes an exhaustive round of bilateral meetings with leaders whose views will be key. These include Germany's Angela Merkel, Russia's Vladimir Putin and Saudi Arabia's Mohammad bin Salman.

En route to Osaka for the G20, Mr Pompeo told The Australian newspaper that Australia had a key role in a global coalition against Iran.

He said this ranged from imposing sanctions of its own to helping ensure free and open navigation through the Straits of Hormuz.

"I think Australia is an important player here. I think they carry a lot of weight in the sense that they, like many nations, suffer from the fact the world's largest state sponsor of terror continues down the path of building its missile program in a way that threatens not only the Middle East but the entire world," Mr Pompeo said.

He said Canberra would be "of great assistance" to US efforts to "build a coalition that will keep those waterways open".

Australia has a long history of sending navy ships to the Persian Gulf for reasons such as enforcing oil export sanctions against Iran and combating piracy and drug smuggling.

The US special envoy to Iran, Brian Hook, has flagged enhancing the 33-nation maritime taskforce - which includes an Australian frigate - currently undertaking anti-drug smuggling and piracy operations in the Persian Gulf and the Arabian Sea.

The Australian Financial Review reported defence experts this week urging Australia to be wary of becoming involved.

Also at the dinner on Thursday night, the Americans expressed their admiration for Australia's strict border protection regime.

Mr Morrison, who "stopped the boats" when he was immigration minister under Tony Abbott, gave a dissertation on how he did it.

While flying to Osaka, Mr Trump tweeted campaign posters the Australian government circulates abroad to discourage people smuggling. "Much can be learned," he said.

Key pointsDonald Trump is mustering international support for any potential military action.

Mike Pompeo says Australia would have a key role in a global coalition.

HEADLINE: Folau and Setka
TEXT:
Rugby union footballer Israel Folau utters a biblical injunction that was standard Christian belief for several millenniums - that gay people are hell-bound if they don't repent - and is fired. CFMEU Victorian secretary John Setka sends vile abuse to his wife for days, and is still in his job with the support of his members. Mr Folau, of course, spoke on Instagram, and Mr Setka in private by text message. But in the age of widespread digital sharing, the boundary lines between public and private communicating have become very blurred.

Mr Folau's views on homosexuality are out of step with mainstream public life in a 21st century secular society. But this does not feel like hate speech. He was merely repeating an ancient doctrine he sincerely believes - as would many Muslims and Jews. He has a right to hardline religious views, even if it makes some uncomfortable. But Rugby Australia has a point too. Mr Folau is well-known only because of rugby, which turns their game into a soapbox for his views that ordinary citizens don't have. They have now taken this pulpit away, and he has sued. It will be a major test of employment law in the modern age.

The episode resonates because an election has just been won by "quiet Australians", many of whom are religious, over noisier activists for LGBTI rights and other causes who would like Mr Folau to remain silent. One third of Australians voted against same-sex marriage, and can't be just dismissed. But it is the genius of liberal democracy that up to a point it tolerates the less tolerant, and is inclusive - a world that progressive activists like to use a lot - of groups that seem to be mutually exclusive.

Mr Setka is in another class. Speech that is intimidatory and threatening is simply its employer's modus operandi. The abuse that he directed at his wife he has directed at others on construction sites. His intent was not peaceful expression but to bully others to his will. The wonder is that the Labor Party had stayed silent for so long. It was only when Mr Setka wandered into the minefield of fashionable gender politics that he got blown up, and because it suited the political interests of some in Labor to get rid of him now.
